scenario: AITA in relation to my GF's attempt to lose weight? | I've been dating my GF for 3 years. She's upset at her current weight. She's put on about 100lbs since we started dating. I've never mentioned it because she has bipolar disorder, and as I struggle with depression I fully understand how food can take the edge off when you get seriously overwhelmed with depression. But for health reasons and of course other reasons, of course I would like for her to get back to a healthy weight. My girlfriend's bipolar disorder has been a challenge for me, as where I would normally be assertive in a relationship on issues - I often have to back down in arguments because she responds poorly to being challenged. I often feel like I'm walking on ice, but I do my best to try understand her and work at helping her and supporting her as best I can. She is not happy with her current weight, and constantly remarks about it and has been complaining about it for over a year without doing anything about it. I tell her we can work on it together as a team, and both fix our diet. I feel this is the best way to go about it, rather than telling her that SHE needs to lose weight. I don't want her feeling like I'm initiating it, or that it's a journey she needs to take alone. Or that I'm pushing her to do it. For it to be a healthy journey, it needs to be something she is motivated to do and if I do it with her, then it doesn't feel like it's all on her. So, last week she decided to work on her diet. She was upset today because she hasn't lost any weight yet. I told her to not worry about the short term results - that it had only been a week, but to focus on months down the line to see changes. She was extremely defeatist and said she'll never lose weight. This kinda irritated me, because it had only been a week since she started. I felt like she hadn't fully committed, because she was drinking soft drinks and eating chips which are high in carbs so I brought that up, if she wants to see results quicker - that cutting out the junk food completely (rather than cutting down) will help her. Now I understand she's trying to make a change, but the defeatist attitude after only a week is difficult to work with. She then got angry at me and told me to "stop arguing with me about my weight". To which I replied that I wasn't, I had never in our entire relationship brought up her weight, and was just discussing her diet and how she was eating and drinking things that will make her progress slower. She then told me to drop it and leave it alone, and is now in a huff with me for the past few hours over it. I understand this is the nature of her bipolar disorder, and she will shut down anything she's challenged about something. Am I the asshole for challenging her defeatist attitude on her results, when she was taking short-cuts with junk food?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm being an asshole in this situation with my girlfriend. Let me start by understanding the scenario. We've been dating for three years, and she's been struggling with her weight, gaining about 100 pounds since we started dating. I know she has bipolar disorder, and I struggle with depression myself, so I understand how food can be a coping mechanism when you're overwhelmed. I've never mentioned her weight because I don't want to hurt her or make things worse, especially considering her mental health challenges. However, I'm concerned about her health and would like her to get back to a healthy weight. I suggested that we work on our diet together as a team, thinking that this approach would be supportive and less pressure on her. I wanted to make sure she didn't feel like I was pushing her or that it was something she had to do alone. I thought this team effort would make the journey healthier and more motivating for her. Last week, she decided to work on her diet. But today, she was upset because she hasn't lost any weight yet. I tried to reassure her that it's only been a week and that she should focus on the long-term changes. I told her not to worry about the short-term results. However, she became very defeatist and said she'll never lose weight. This frustrated me because it had only been a week since she started. I felt like she wasn't fully committed because she was still drinking soft drinks and eating chips, which are high in carbs. So, I brought that up, suggesting that if she wants to see quicker results, she should cut out junk food completely instead of just cutting down. Now, she got angry at me and told me to "stop arguing with me about my weight." I replied that I wasn't bringing up her weight and that I was just discussing her diet and how she was eating and drinking things that would slow her progress. She then told me to drop it and leave it alone and is now upset with me for the past few hours. I understand that this is part of her bipolar disorder, and she shuts down when she feels challenged about something. So, the question is: Am I the asshole for challenging her defeatist attitude about her results when she was taking shortcuts with junk food? First, I need to consider the dynamics of our relationship. I've been supportive and understanding of her mental health struggles, and I've never brought up her weight before. I suggested working on our diet together to make it a team effort, which I thought was a good approach. However, when she became defeatist after only a week, I tried to encourage her by pointing out that her diet choices were hindering her progress. On one hand, I can see that I was trying to support her and help her achieve her goals. I wanted to provide constructive feedback to help her be more successful in her weight loss journey. On the other hand, I can understand why she got upset. She might have felt criticized or judged, especially since she's dealing with bipolar disorder and is already sensitive to being challenged. I also need to think about how my approach might have come across. Even though I intended to be supportive, my suggestion to cut out junk food completely might have been perceived as pushy or critical. She might have felt that I was focusing on her shortcomings rather than her efforts. Additionally, I should consider the timing of my feedback. She was already feeling defeated after a week, and bringing up her diet choices might have added to her frustration. It might have been better to acknowledge her feelings first and then gently suggest ways to improve her diet without making her feel like she was failing. I also need to reflect on how I responded when she got angry. I tried to clarify that I wasn't talking about her weight but her diet, but she still felt upset. Maybe I should have approached the conversation differently, focusing more on her feelings and less on the specifics of her diet. In the end, I want to support her without making her feel criticized or judged. I need to find a balance between offering encouragement and providing constructive feedback without overstepping or making her feel like she's being nagged. So, considering all this, I think I might have been a bit too direct in my feedback, which could have come across as pushy or critical, especially given her sensitivity due to her bipolar disorder. While my intentions were good, the way I delivered the feedback might have been the issue. I should have been more empathetic and understanding of her feelings before bringing up the diet changes. Therefore, I might have been the asshole in this situation by not considering her emotional state and the way I presented my feedback. I should have approached the conversation with more sensitivity and understanding, focusing on her feelings first before discussing the diet changes.
